title: 1 Kings 6:23–38
context: 1 Kings 6:23–38 describes the two great cherubim of olive wood in the inner sanctuary, each ten cubits high, with wings stretching from wall to wall and touching in the middle, all overlaid with gold. Cherubim are angelic beings. The walls are carved with cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, and the floors and doors are covered with gold. The section ends by noting that the foundation was laid in the month Ziv of Solomon’s fourth year and the house was finished in the month Bul of the eleventh year, seven years in all. Many interpreters in both traditions see the cherubim and garden imagery as recalling Eden and the cherubim over the ark (Genesis 3:24; Exodus 25:18–22), and both read the chapter as celebrating God’s dwelling among his people.

verses.text: In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olive wood, each ten cubits high.
verses.arminianNotes: In the inner sanctuary he makes two cherubim of olive wood, each ten cubits high. Cherubim are angelic beings. Arminian readers see the cherubim as guardians of God’s presence, a possible recollection of those placed at Eden (Genesis 3:24).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the connection with the cherubim on the ark’s cover (Exodus 25:18–22). Both traditions see the large cherubim as expressing God’s holiness and majesty, and both avoid speculating beyond what Scripture says about them.

verses.text: Five cubits was the length of one wing of the cherub, and five cubits was the length of the other wing of the cherub. From the tip of one wing to the tip of the other was ten cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: Each cherub’s wings are five cubits, ten cubits from tip to tip. Arminians read the measurements as describing the grand size of the cherubim, which fill the inner sanctuary as symbols of God’s throne and presence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and treat the measurements as description rather than as a point of disagreement. Both traditions read the verse as part of a careful account of the most holy place.

verses.text: The other cherub was ten cubits. Both the cherubim were of one measure and one form.
verses.arminianNotes: The other cherub is also ten cubits, and both have the same measure and form. Arminian readers see the symmetry of the two cherubim as part of the order and beauty that characterizes God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The repetition emphasizes that the two cherubim matched exactly. Both traditions treat the verse as architectural detail, read in the context of the whole description of the most holy place.

verses.text: One cherub was ten cubits high, and so was the other cherub.
verses.arminianNotes: One cherub is ten cubits high, and so is the other. Arminians see the repetition of the measurements as the narrator’s careful emphasis on the matching pair, part of the precise record of the temple’s construction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see no theological contrast in the detail. Both traditions read the verse as completing the description of the cherubim’s height before the next verse describes their position.

verses.text: He set the cherubim within the inner house. The wings of the cherubim were stretched out, so that the wing of the one touched the one wall and the wing of the other cherub touched the other wall; and their wings touched one another in the middle of the house.
verses.arminianNotes: The cherubim stand in the inner house with outstretched wings touching the walls on each side and each other in the middle. Arminian readers see the wings spanning the room as a picture of God’s presence filling and guarding the most holy place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the ark will be placed beneath these wings (1 Kings 8:6–7). Both traditions see the arrangement as expressing God’s throne among his people, the LORD who sits above the cherubim (2 Samuel 6:2).

verses.text: He overlaid the cherubim with gold.
verses.arminianNotes: He overlays the cherubim with gold. Arminians see the gold as extending the glory of the inner sanctuary to the cherubim, which together express the majesty of God’s presence among his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and read the verse as completing the description of the cherubim. Both traditions see the gold overlay as consistent with the splendor of the whole house and avoid adding symbolism the text does not give.

verses.text: He carved all the walls of the house around with carved figures of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, inside and outside.
verses.arminianNotes: He carves the walls all around with cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, inside and outside. Arminian readers see the carvings as surrounding worshipers with images of God’s presence and life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Many interpreters see the combination of cherubim and plant imagery as recalling Eden, offered as a possible connection rather than a certainty. Both traditions read the verse as celebrating the beauty of the house God chose.

verses.text: He overlaid the floor of the house with gold, inside and outside.
verses.arminianNotes: He overlays the floor with gold, inside and outside. Arminians see the extent of the gold as underscoring the glory of the temple, with even the floor covered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. Interpreters discuss whether "inside and outside" means the inner sanctuary and the main hall. Both traditions treat the verse as description of the temple’s splendor without theological dispute.

verses.text: For the entrance of the inner sanctuary, he made doors of olive wood. The lintel and door posts were a fifth part of the wall.
verses.arminianNotes: For the entrance to the inner sanctuary he makes doors of olive wood, with the lintel and doorposts a fifth part of the wall. Arminian readers see the entrance to the most holy place marked with care, since access to God’s presence was restricted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The phrase "a fifth part" is uncertain and may describe the shape or proportion of the doorway. Both traditions treat it as architectural detail and read the restricted entrance in light of Hebrews 9:7–8.

verses.text: So he made two doors of olive wood; and he carved on them carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, and overlaid them with gold. He spread the gold on the cherubim and on the palm trees.
verses.arminianNotes: The two olive wood doors are carved with cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers and overlaid with gold. Arminians see the same imagery as the walls repeated on the doors, so the whole house shares one design.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the doors as part of the consistent symbolism of the temple. Both traditions read the verse as description that highlights the beauty and holiness of the entrance to the most holy place.

verses.text: He also made the entrance of the temple door posts of olive wood, out of a fourth part of the wall,
verses.arminianNotes: He makes the doorposts of the temple entrance of olive wood, a fourth part of the wall. Arminian readers see the main entrance to the temple also crafted with care, though less elaborately than the entrance to the inner sanctuary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. As in 6:31, the meaning of the proportion is uncertain. Both traditions treat the verse as architectural description, noting the gradation of holiness from the main entrance to the inner sanctuary.

verses.text: and two doors of cypress wood. The two leaves of the one door were folding, and the two leaves of the other door were folding.
verses.arminianNotes: The two cypress doors each have two folding leaves. Arminians see practical design in the folding doors, which made the large entrance usable for regular worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and treat the verse as construction detail. Both traditions read the description of the doors as part of the account of a house built with both beauty and practical function.

verses.text: He carved cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers; and he overlaid them with gold fitted on the engraved work.
verses.arminianNotes: He carves cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers and overlays them with gold fitted to the carvings. Arminian readers see the same pattern carried through the main doors, showing a unified design for the whole house of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the careful fitting of gold to the carved surface. Both traditions read the verse as completing the description of the doors without adding symbolism the text does not state.

verses.text: He built the inner court with three courses of cut stone and a course of cedar beams.
verses.arminianNotes: He builds the inner court with three courses of cut stone and a course of cedar beams. Arminians see the court as the space around the house where priests served, separated from the outer areas.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the same construction method appears in 1 Kings 7:12. Both traditions treat the verse as architectural description and avoid speculation about the exact layout of the courts.

verses.text: The foundation of the LORD’s house was laid in the fourth year, in the month Ziv.
verses.arminianNotes: The foundation of the LORD’s house was laid in the fourth year, in the month Ziv. Arminian readers see the narrator returning to the date given in 6:1, framing the building account with its beginning and end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the frame as marking the careful record of the work. Both traditions note that Ziv is identified in 6:1 as the second month, and they read the verse as a summary before the completion notice.

verses.text: In the eleventh year, in the month Bul, which is the eighth month, the house was finished throughout all its parts and according to all its specifications. So he spent seven years building it.
verses.arminianNotes: In the eleventh year, in the month Bul, the eighth month, the house was finished in every part, seven years in building. Arminians see faithful completion of the work God had promised, carried out in full according to the plan.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the house was finished "according to all its specifications." Some see significance in the seven years, and both traditions offer that cautiously. Both read the verse as God’s promise to David fulfilled through Solomon’s work.
